title: Structure-Function Correlation in Diabetic Retinal Disease using Innovative High-Resolution Imaging and Lesion-Specific Microperimetry.
summary: Diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of blindness in the working age population. It is a complex disease that leads to nerve damage, inflammation and problems with the small blood vessels in the eye - often long before people notice any deterioration in their vision. The problem is that the disease is usually treated after significant retinal damage has occurred. This makes it difficult to prevent vision loss at an early stage. The severity of the disease is often determined by best corrected visual acuity. However, this does not always accurately reflect the true extent of retinal damage. Modern imaging techniques such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT angiography can help to better assess risk. They provide valuable information about structural changes in the retina. The aim of this project is to find out how certain retinal characteristics measured by OCT and OCT angiography are related to macular pigment optical density (MPOD). It will also investigate whether diet has an effect on macular pigment in people with diabetes. A special examination technique - personalized microperimetry - will also help to establish a more precise relationship between retinal changes and actual visual function.

interventions.name:
Diabetics with or without diabetic retinopathy / maculopathy 

Multimodality imaging using conventional SD-OCT, OCTA, MPOD and High-resolution OCT is performed every 3 to 6 months for 3 years.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Consenting patients with type I/II diabetes mellitus
Exclusion criteria:
Other previous retinal diseases (age-related macular degeneration, glaucoma, retinal vascular occlusion) and/or inadequate quality of imaging
